A turbine is a machine that spins when a moving fluid — either a gas (like air or steam) or a liquid (like water) — flows over its blades. That spinning motion is then used to do useful work, most often to generate electricity or to power vehicles.

The central principle is beautifully simple: a fluid in motion carries energy. A turbine captures that energy by letting the moving fluid push against specially shaped blades, causing them to rotate. That rotation is the turbine's output.
A Simple Picture in Your Mind

Imagine holding a pinwheel toy in front of a fan. The moving air pushes the angled blades, and the pinwheel spins. A turbine works on exactly that same idea — but with much greater power and precision.

A better real-world comparison is an old waterwheel at a flour mill. A river's current pushed wooden paddles on a wheel, the wheel spun, and that spinning motion was used to grind grain. A turbine is a far more refined and efficient version of that same concept.
The Key Parts of a Turbine

Every turbine has three essential components.

The blades (sometimes called vanes or buckets) are the curved surfaces that the fluid pushes against. Their shape is carefully engineered — similar in principle to an airplane wing — so that when fluid flows past them, they are pushed in one rotational direction with maximum efficiency.

The rotor is the central shaft and hub to which all the blades are attached. When the blades are pushed by the fluid, the rotor spins. This spinning shaft is the mechanical output of the turbine — the thing that does the work downstream.

The casing (or housing) is the outer shell that surrounds the rotor and guides the fluid in a controlled, directed manner onto the blades, ensuring as little energy as possible is wasted.
How a Turbine Works — Step by Step

First, a fluid under pressure or at high speed is directed into the turbine housing and steered precisely onto the blades. Second, as the fluid strikes or flows across the curved blades, it exerts a push (a force) on them. Because the blades are fixed to the rotor, this force makes the rotor spin. Third, as the fluid gives up its energy to the blades, it slows down, loses pressure, and exits the turbine. Fourth, the now-spinning rotor shaft is connected to whatever needs to be powered — most commonly an electrical generator, which converts that rotational motion into electricity.

All turbines are driven by one of two categories of fluid.

Gases — including steam, hot combustion gases, or wind. These are compressible, meaning they can be squeezed, which engineers use to their advantage.

Liquids — primarily water. Liquids are far denser than gases, which means even a slow-moving liquid carries a great deal of force, making liquid-driven turbines extremely powerful.

Steam turbines are the most widely used turbines on Earth. Water is heated (by burning coal, natural gas, or through nuclear fission) to produce high-pressure steam, which is blasted onto the turbine's blades. These are the engines inside most of the world's conventional power plants.

Gas turbines are driven by the hot, high-pressure gases produced when fuel is burned. The jet engines on aircraft are gas turbines — they don't just spin a generator; they also pull in air from the front and blast it out the back at speed, which produces the thrust that moves the plane forward.

Water turbines (also called hydraulic turbines) are driven by flowing or falling water. Inside a hydroelectric dam, enormous volumes of water fall from a great height and rush through tunnels, striking the turbine blades with tremendous force. The Hoover Dam and the Three Gorges Dam in China are examples of massive hydroelectric facilities that use these.

Wind turbines are the large three-bladed structures you see on wind farms. Moving air turns their long blades, which are connected through a shaft to a generator high up inside the tower. These convert the natural kinetic energy of wind into electricity.
What Turbines Power in the Real World

The single biggest use of turbines is generating electricity. The vast majority of the world's electrical power — whether it comes from a coal plant, a nuclear plant, a natural gas plant, a hydroelectric dam, or a wind farm — is produced by a turbine spinning a generator. In that sense, almost every time you switch on a light or charge your phone, a turbine is involved somewhere up the chain.

Beyond electricity, turbines power commercial aircraft (jet engines), propel large naval ships, and appear in turbochargers inside high-performance car engines, where a small turbine driven by exhaust gases forces extra air into the engine to boost its power.

Turbines are among the most consequential inventions in human history. Modern civilization's electrical grid — the infrastructure that powers hospitals, homes, industry, communications, and transportation — is almost entirely built on turbine technology. Without turbines, large-scale electricity generation as we know it would not exist.
A turbine is a rotating machine that converts the energy of a moving fluid into mechanical energy, typically to generate electricity or to power vehicles.
